# Incident Report: MTA-2026-01-31 Traffic Analysis

## 1. Victim Host

| Attribute | Value | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| IPv4 address | **10.1.21.58** | Consistent source across DHCP, NBNS, Kerberos, ARP |
| MAC address | **00:21:5d:c8:0e:f2** | Confirmed via ARP request/reply pairs (`who-has 10.1.21.58` / `is-at 00:21:5d:c8:0e:f2`), matches DHCP client and NBNS source |
| Windows hostname | **DESKTOP-ES9F3ML** | DHCP Option 12 hostname (frames 1/3), NBNS `<00>`/`<20>` name registration, mDNS query |
| AD domain | WIN11OFFICE.COM (NetBIOS: WIN11OFFICE) | Kerberos realm, NBNS domain name records, LDAP/CLDAP to DC |
| Logged-in user | **gwyatt** | Kerberos AS-REQ/TGS-REQ `CNameString = gwyatt`, realm `WIN11OFFICE.COM`, exchanged with DC 10.1.21.2 (MAC 14:b3:1f:2d:ce:69) |

Gateway for reference: 10.1.21.1, MAC 00:04:c1:be:8c:d4.

## 2. Malware Family

**Assessment: consistent with a commodity loader / Pay-Per-Install (PPI)-style downloader with a browser-hijack/fingerprinting check-in component ("ChromeLoader"-class behavior).**

**Attribution basis: behavioral only — not signature-confirmed.** The evidence directory contains only the pcap; no Suricata/IDS alert export was provided, so no rule-hit/signature match exists to cite. The call below is built entirely from observed protocol behavior:

- Victim resolves and connects to two typo-squatted "file hosting" domains (`hiyter.com`, `media.megafilehub4.lat`) within the same second window, then immediately fetches a large (~16 MB) object from a third similarly-named domain (`arch.filemegahab4.sbs`) — a pattern typical of fake download-portal / SEO-poisoning malware delivery rather than legitimate browsing.
- That payload fetch is fronted by Cloudflare and negotiated with **Encrypted Client Hello (ECH)** (outer SNI = the ECH placeholder `cloudflare-ech.com`), hiding the true destination at the TLS layer — an evasion technique, not standard behavior for the rest of the host's normal Microsoft/Google/CDN traffic on this capture.
- Roughly 20–75 seconds after the download completes, the host begins repeated check-ins to `whitepepper.su` over **both port 80 (plaintext HTTP) and port 443**, hitting an endpoint `/api/set_agent` that carries an `id=`/`token=` pair and cycles a spoofed `agent=Chrome` / `agent=Edge` parameter, then POSTs (`act=log`) a very large, gzip-compressed fingerprint blob containing Canvas hash, WebGL renderer string, installed fonts, audio-context parameters, screen/hardware info, and a `webdriver:false` check — classic anti-bot/anti-sandbox browser fingerprinting used by malware "gates" and PPI-loader panels to validate real victims before further tasking.
- The same infection window also touches several other freshly-registered-looking, thematically unrelated domains (`whooptm.cyou`, `communicationfirewall-security.cc`, `holiday-forever.cc`), consistent with a multi-domain C2/redirector infrastructure rather than a single legitimate service.

No AV/EDR alert, malware sample, or file hash was present in the evidence to allow a hash-based or rule-based confirmation — hence **behavioral, not signature-confirmed**.

## 3. Indicators of Compromise (grounded in captured traffic)

### Malicious domains
| Domain | Resolved IP(s) | First seen (rel. sec) | Role |
|---|---|---|---|
| hiyter.com | 104.21.22.231, 172.67.207.145 | 45.3s | Initial landing/redirect page |
| media.megafilehub4.lat | 104.21.48.156, 172.67.154.67 | 45.8s | Initial landing/redirect page |
| arch.filemegahab4.sbs | 104.21.46.67, 172.67.136.13 | 48.3s | Payload host (16 MB TLS transfer, ECH-obscured SNI) |
| whitepepper.su | 153.92.1.49 | 92.3s (first HTTP request 24500) | C2/fingerprint check-in panel |
| whooptm.cyou | 62.72.32.156 | 90.3s | C2/redirector infrastructure |
| holiday-forever.cc | 80.97.160.24 | 122.8s | C2/redirector infrastructure |
| communicationfirewall-security.cc | 104.21.9.36, 172.67.141.109 | 126.5s | C2/redirector infrastructure |

### Command-and-control endpoints (IP:port)
- **153.92.1.49:80** and **153.92.1.49:443** — whitepepper.su, primary C2/fingerprint-logging endpoint
- 62.72.32.156:443 — whooptm.cyou
- 80.97.160.24:443 — holiday-forever.cc
- 104.21.9.36:443 — communicationfirewall-security.cc
- 104.21.46.67:443 — arch.filemegahab4.sbs (payload delivery)
- 104.21.48.156:443 — media.megafilehub4.lat

### Malicious URLs (observed cleartext requests)
```
http://whitepepper.su/api/set_agent?id=3BF67EC05320C5729578BE4C0ADF174C&token=842e2802df0f0a06b4ed51f12f4387e761523b&description=&agent=Chrome
http://whitepepper.su/api/set_agent?id=3BF67EC05320C5729578BE4C0ADF174C&token=842e2802df0f0a06b4ed51f12f4387e761523b&description=&agent=Chrome&act=log
http://whitepepper.su/api/set_agent?id=3BF67EC05320C5729578BE4C0ADF174C&token=842e2802df0f0a06b4ed51f12f4387e761523b&description=&agent=Edge
http://whitepepper.su/api/set_agent?id=3BF67EC05320C5729578BE4C0ADF174C&token=842e2802df0f0a06b4ed51f12f4387e761523b&description=&agent=Edge&act=log
```
Bot/campaign identifiers used in the above: `id=3BF67EC05320C5729578BE4C0ADF174C`, `token=842e2802df0f0a06b4ed51f12f4387e761523b`.

### Transferred files / hashes
None recoverable. The only bulk transfer (~16 MB, arch.filemegahab4.sbs, 104.21.46.67:443, 48.3s–70.7s) was carried entirely inside TLS with no decryption keys available in the evidence, so its filename and SHA256 cannot be determined from this capture. No cleartext HTTP file/binary transfer occurred anywhere in the pcap — the only classic-HTTP objects present are the two whitepepper.su fingerprint payloads (JSON/urlencoded text, not executables), a Microsoft NCSI `connecttest.txt`, and a Google time-sync response, none of which are malicious artifacts themselves.

## 4. Recommended next steps
- Isolate 10.1.21.58 (DESKTOP-ES9F3ML, user gwyatt) from the network pending forensic imaging.
- Obtain disk/memory image or EDR telemetry to identify the actual dropped binary and compute a SHA256 — network evidence alone cannot supply this due to TLS/ECH.
- Block/sinkhole the domains and IPs listed above at the perimeter.
- Reset gwyatt's domain credentials given the AD/Kerberos activity observed from the infected host during the incident window.
